title: Checkout and the order state machine
subtitle: Give every order a clear list of states and allowed moves, so checkout stays correct when payments time out, webhooks arrive late and stock runs out.

c.v: This is a made-up story, but each failure in it is common.
Ravi's team runs a shoe shop. On a sale day, the payment provider was slow. The checkout service called "authorize payment" with a 3-second
The code treated a timeout as a decline. It marked those orders "failed" and released the stock. The app showed "Payment failed, please try again". Many buyers tapped Pay again.
But many first payments had worked. The provider just answered late. Its
arrived a minute later, saying the payments succeeded. The webhook handler set those orders to "paid", even though they were "failed" and their stock was gone.
So some buyers paid twice for one pair of shoes. Some "paid" orders had no stock, so the warehouse could not ship them. Support spent two weeks on refunds.

Write the allowed moves in one table, in one place in the code. Every change goes through one function that checks the table. A webhook, an admin tool and a cron job all use that same function.
Make illegal moves impossible, not just unlikely. One transition table, one function that changes state, and one history row for every change.

Do not hold a database transaction open while you call the provider. Airbnb's library splits each request into three parts. It saves the request, makes the network call, then saves the result.
The two database parts never make network calls, and the network call never touches the database. Airbnb learned that network calls inside those database parts can quickly use up the

It may remove keys after they are at least 24 hours old. It also returns an error if a retry sends different parameters.
Use one provider key per payment attempt, for example

makes sure payment 1234 is refunded only once.
A timeout does not mean "declined". Airbnb's library sorts errors into retryable and non-retryable. Network and server errors (5XX) are retryable. Invalid requests (4XX) are not.
On a retry, it can first ask the downstream service for the transaction's status.

Keep timeouts short, too. Shopify suggests starting with a 1-second connect timeout and a 5-second read timeout, then tuning from your own data.
Webhooks: late, repeated and out of order
Stripe does not promise to send events in the order they happened.
It also says not to use an event's
time to order events. Track event IDs to find duplicates, and fetch the latest object from the API when you need it.
So the webhook handler should not set a state directly. It reads the payment's current status and asks the guard for a move. A late success for a
order is refused. If the payment is only authorized (

, refund it, because a succeeded payment can't be cancelled. Log both cases.
Stripe also says your fulfilment code may be called many times, even at the same moment, for one Checkout Session.
Snapshot prices, then handle partial work
When you create the order, copy the unit price, discount, tax, currency and shipping fee onto each order line. Store money as integers in
. Later price changes must not change old orders, receipts or refunds.

Partial shipments need care. On Stripe, most payments allow only one capture, and a partial capture releases the rest.
So capture once, then refund items that never ship. Stripe allows several refunds on one charge, but never more than the original amount in total.
Keep shipments and refunds as their own rows that point to order lines, instead of adding more order states.

q.v: A buyer taps Place order. The app's request times out, and the app retries. How do you stop a second order and a second charge?

options.v: Ask the buyer to wait 30 seconds before tapping again.
The app creates one idempotency key per checkout and sends the same key on every retry. The server returns the order it already made.
The server creates a new order and refunds the old one later.

why.v: The key lets the server spot the repeat. Stripe works the same way and returns the saved result for a repeated key.

q.v: Your call to authorize a payment times out. What should your code do next?

options.v: Mark the order failed and release the stock at once.
Send a new payment request with a new idempotency key.
Treat the result as unknown. Ask the provider about this order, or retry with the same key, before you decide.

why.v: A timeout does not mean the charge failed. A new key could charge the card twice. Airbnb's library can ask for the status first when it retries.

q.v: A payment_intent.succeeded webhook arrives for an order that is already cancelled. What should happen?

options.v: Move the order back to confirmed and ship it.
The transition guard refuses the move. You refund the payment and alert someone.
Ignore the webhook and keep the money.

why.v: Cancelled is a final state, so no rule allows cancelled to confirmed. A succeeded payment can't be cancelled, so you refund it.

q.v: An order has two items. One ships today, one ships in 10 days. You authorized the card at checkout. On Stripe, what is the risk of capturing per shipment?

options.v: None. You can capture as many times as you like.
For most payments you can capture only once. A partial capture releases the rest, and a card hold usually lasts about 7 days.
Stripe captures both parts for you.

why.v: Stripe says most payments allow one capture, and a partial capture releases the remaining amount. Capture once, then refund what never ships.

q.v: Why do you copy the price and tax onto the order line when the order is placed?

options.v: So a later price change does not change what the buyer agreed to pay, refunds or receipts.
Because the product table can't store prices.

why.v: The catalogue changes over time. The order is a record of one deal at one moment, so it keeps its own copy.
